title: Spring Lecture #17: Spring Boot Exception Handling: Make Your APIs Professional

questions.question: A client posts a well-formed student whose email format is valid, but a student with that email already exists. Which status code does the lecture use?
options: 400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: The request itself is valid; it conflicts with existing server data, which is what 409 Conflict means, and the code throws `DuplicateResourceException` mapped to `HttpStatus.CONFLICT`. 400 is for requests that are themselves invalid, such as a malformed email or `"age":"twenty"`.
questions.source: notes p11-p13, p45-p47; code: StudentService.java, GlobalExceptionHandler.java

questions.question: Why does the lecture's `GlobalExceptionHandler` use `@RestControllerAdvice` rather than plain `@ControllerAdvice`?
options: It is `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody`, so handler return values are written as the JSON response body instead of being resolved as views
It is the only annotation that lets `@ExceptionHandler` methods run at all
It makes the class handle exceptions only from `@RestController` classes in the same package
It turns every handler's status into 500 unless overridden
questions.explanation: The notes describe `@RestControllerAdvice` as a shortcut for `@ControllerAdvice` plus `@ResponseBody`, which suits REST APIs returning JSON. `@ExceptionHandler` methods also work inside a plain `@ControllerAdvice`; the difference is only how return values are treated.

questions.question: Your delete API removes the student successfully and there is nothing meaningful to send back. Which return statement matches the lecture's preferred REST style?
options: `return ResponseEntity.ok(null);`
`return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).build();`
`return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();`
`return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();`
questions.explanation: `noContent().build()` returns 204 No Content: success with no body, which the notes say is often preferred for deletes (200 with a message is the other common option). 201 is for creating a resource, and 404 would wrongly tell the client the student did not exist.

questions.question: `GET /api/students/99` calls the service below and student 99 does not exist. The lecture's advice class has these handlers. What status does the client receive?
options: 500, because the `RuntimeException` handler is declared and matches too
404, because Spring picks the handler whose exception type is closest to the thrown exception
500, because the `Exception` handler catches everything
Startup fails, because three handlers match the same exception
questions.explanation: All three handlers could match, but Spring sorts candidates by exception depth and uses the most specific one, `ResourceNotFoundException`, giving 404 with the error DTO. Broader handlers are fallbacks only, and overlapping handler types are allowed.
questions.source: notes p33-p34, p37-p38; code: GlobalExceptionHandler.java, StudentService.java

questions.question: Which create-API return statement sends 201 Created together with a `Location: /api/students/10` header and the saved student as the body?
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: `ResponseEntity.created(location)` sets status 201 and the `Location` header in one call, and `.body(savedStudent)` adds the body. A sends 200, B has no header or body, and D is a 204 without the student, even though it sets a location.

questions.question: A service uses `studentRepository.findById(id).get()` and the app has no `@RestControllerAdvice`. Postman calls `GET /api/students/2` for a student that does not exist. What does it get, and what is wrong with that?
options: Spring Boot's default `/error` JSON with status 500 "Internal Server Error", which is misleading because the real situation is a missing resource (404)
404 Not Found automatically, because Spring knows `Optional` means "not found"
200 OK with a `null` body, because `.get()` returns null for an empty Optional
400 Bad Request, because the id does not exist
questions.explanation: `.get()` on an empty `Optional` throws `NoSuchElementException`; with no handler, Boot forwards to its default `/error` mapping, which reports 500. The lecture's point is that this is not a server crash but a missing student, so the service should throw `ResourceNotFoundException` and a global handler should map it to 404. Spring has no built-in rule that turns an empty Optional into 404 here.

questions.question: The lecture's `application.properties` contains `spring.web.error.include-message=always`, yet the notes recommend that the generic `Exception` handler return a fixed text such as "Something went wrong. Please try again later." instead of `ex.getMessage()`. What is the reasoning?
options: Exception messages are always empty in production, so a fixed text is needed
`include-message=always` is required for `@ExceptionHandler` methods to run
Fixed texts make the response faster because no exception object is created
Boot hides exception messages by default for safety; including them helps local learning, but raw messages of unexpected errors can leak internal details in production
questions.explanation: The notes say Boot's default error response hides detailed messages, `include-message=always` shows them for learning, and internal exception messages should not be exposed in production. Hence the fallback handler should return a generic "Something went wrong" message. The property only affects Boot's default `/error` response, not whether your own handlers run.

questions.question: The lecture's code (not the notes' final version) has exactly these handlers. A client posts `{"name":"Amit","age":"twenty",...}` to `POST /api/students`. What does it receive?
options: 400 with `fieldErrors` saying age must be a number
500 from the `RuntimeException` handler, carrying a JSON parse error message
400 from Spring's default handling, because invalid JSON is always a client error
201, because Jackson converts "twenty" to 0
questions.explanation: "twenty" cannot become an `Integer`, so Spring throws `HttpMessageNotReadableException` before validation even runs; `MethodArgumentNotValidException` is never thrown. Because that exception is a `RuntimeException` and the advice has a `RuntimeException` handler, that handler wins and returns 500. The notes fix this with a dedicated `HttpMessageNotReadableException` handler returning 400.

questions.question: A client sends `"name": ""`. `name` has both `@NotBlank(message = "Name cannot be null/Empty or blank")` and `@Size(min = 2, max = 50, message = "Student name must be within 2 to 50 character long")`. What does `fieldErrors` contain for `name`?
options: Both messages, stored as a list under the key `name`
Only the `@NotBlank` message, because validation stops at the first failed constraint on a field
Exactly one of the two messages: both constraints fail, but `put` with the same key overwrites, and the order of the field errors is not guaranteed
No entry, because an empty string is not null
questions.explanation: An empty string violates `@NotBlank` and also `@Size(min = 2)`, so there are two `FieldError`s for `name`. A `Map<String, String>` keyed by field name keeps only the last `put`, and Bean Validation does not promise an order, so the surviving message is not deterministic. Collecting a `List<String>` per field would keep both.

questions.question: With the lecture's handler set (including `RuntimeException` and `Exception` handlers), `GET /api/students/abc` returns 500 because `"abc"` cannot be converted to the `Long` id. You want 400 instead. What is the right change?
options: Delete the `RuntimeException` handler so Spring's default 400 handling takes over
Add `@Valid` before `@PathVariable Long id`
Change the parameter type to `String` and let the repository convert it
Add an `@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException.class)` method returning 400 with the error DTO
questions.explanation: The failed conversion throws `MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException`, a `RuntimeException` subclass, so a dedicated handler for it becomes the closest match and can return 400, exactly as the notes show. Deleting the `RuntimeException` handler does not help, because the `Exception` handler would still catch it and return 500. `@Valid` checks constraints and cannot fix type conversion.
